title: Anthropic and NTT Data in final talks on $6.3B Osaka data center
subtitle: Nikkei Asia reports a 500 MW first-in-Japan Anthropic site, with construction up to ¥1 trillion and partial operations targeted for 2028; both companies declined to comment.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: NTT Data is in the final stages of talks to build Anthropic's first dedicated data center in Japan, located in Osaka, according to Nikkei Asia reporting dated October 13 and relayed by Reuters. Construction alone could run up to ¥1 trillion (about $6.3 billion), with the full project — once advanced AI servers and their chip complement are installed — pushing the total investment into the several-trillion-yen range. The companies aim to sign a formal agreement by the end of NTT Data's fiscal 2026, which closes in March 2027.

The planned site is sized at 500 megawatts, with partial operations targeted for as early as 2028. Drawing that much power from the Japanese grid is slow, so Nikkei reports the project will first explore on-site generation and fuel cells rather than wait on utility-scale interconnection. That is now a standard pattern — the US Oracle–We Energies nuclear deal for OpenAI in Wisconsin, Meta's 5 GW Hyperion build in Louisiana, and Anthropic's Theseus joint venture with Macquarie and GIC earlier this year all route around grid timelines using behind-the-meter supply.

For Anthropic specifically, a 500 MW Japanese site is the second major non-US compute commitment it has set up this quarter after its reported Volta/Bitdeer Norway deal, and it fits the pattern of a lab that has been scaling capex aggressively ahead of a reported October–November IPO window. The Osaka location, rather than Tokyo, matches NTT Data's existing western-Japan footprint and avoids the earthquake-and-density constraints of Kanto-region builds. Both Anthropic and NTT Data declined to comment to Nikkei, so the specifics should be read as reported, not confirmed.

For learners: data center siting is now a first-order AI story, not a sub-plot. The real constraints are not GPU allocations — they are 500 MW power contracts, land near fiber trunks, water for cooling, and local regulatory sign-off. Any time you see a lab announce 'we will build a new frontier model,' quietly check who is building the physical facility that will train it. The second announcement often tells you more about the first than the model paper does.
